newsitem.title: USA: U.S. East Coast braces for Fran's arrival.
newsitem.headline: U.S. East Coast braces for Fran's arrival.

text.p: Heavy rain and gusty winds pelted the U.S. mid-Atlantic coast on Thursday as police went door-to-door in beach areas to evacuate residents ahead of Hurricane Fran and its dangerous 115 mph (185 kmh) winds.

Fran wobbled slightly northward, making its landfall most likely along the beach communities near the North and South Carolina border late on Thursday or early on Friday, the National Hurricane Centre said.

In North Carolina, Governor James Hunt on Thursday declared a state of emergency for all the state's 100 counties and said evacuation orders were in effect for more than 500,000 residents and tourists in the state.

"This is a very powerful storm and it is veering toward our coast," Hunt said. "It will come inland apparently in North Carolina, rather than South Carolina, and it is just immense in terms of its width. It is almost going to cover the whole state."
It was the first time that a state of emergency was ever declared for all 100 North Carolina counties, Hunt said.
"We've had tremendous flooding in the west. We've had 11 inches (28 cm) of rain in 12 hours. We've got roads washed out, and this is going to come on top of that," Hunt said.

Fran was predicted to cut across the heart of North Carolina, dumping up to 10 inches (25 cms) of rain in its path and flooding coastal neighbourhoods and inland areas that were still soaked from recent heavy rains. Dangerous storm surges of more than 10 feet (3 metres) were also expected.
Police travelled on coastal highways to evacuate residents from barrier islands and beaches.
"We've had good cooperation so far," said Lt. Vince Ward of the Myrtle Beach police department. "The roads leading away from here were jammed with people yesterday. Today they're empty."

Residents of Charleston, an historic port city battered seven years ago by Hurricane Hugo, sighed with relief as forecasters said Fran's course would put the eye about 100 miles (160 km) north. The full brunt of Fran's 115 mph winds (185 kmh) were predicted to make landfall late on Thursday evening.
Mandatory evacuations were ordered in many of North Carolina's southernmost coastal communities as Fran took a more northward track.

Officials predicted that Fran would create a storm surge up to 16 feet (4.8 metres) early on Friday along part of the coast, threatening billions of dollars of beachfront development. Fuelling the surge will be high tide at 3 a.m. EDT (1900 GMT) on Friday, when the worst of Fran's 115 mph (185 kmh) winds were to be blowing inland.

Some school systems cancelled classes on Thursday as far as 100 miles (160 km) inland, when forecasters predicted Hurricane force winds could strike as far west as Florence, South Carolina, and Fayetteville, North Carolina.
Nursing homes took the elderly to shelters or called relatives to collect them and emergency teams worked overnight to pull down roadside billboards.

At 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT), the centre of Fran was about 170 miles (275 km) south-southeast of Myrtle Beach. Fran picked up a little speed during the night and was moving north-northwest at 14 mph (22 kmh).
At Cape Canaveral, about halfway up the Florida coast, NASA rolled the space shuttle Atlantis back to its massive garage as a precaution against storm conditions, delaying its takeoff.
